description: Burnout isn’t an individual problem—it’s a systemic design issue that shows up differently across the organization chart. Early-career employees burn out from ambiguity and lack of control, managers from “responsibility without authority,” executives from value conflicts and moral strain, and founders from over-identifying with their mission. Across all levels, the root cause tends to be not workload alone but unclear priorities, misaligned incentives, and poor decision structures. Generic fixes like resilience training miss the point; effective leaders prevent burnout by redesigning work. To address burnout proactively before it takes root, leaders need to understand how it can show up, why it happens, and what they can do to help.
title: Burnout Looks Different Across the Org Chart. Watch for These Signs.

description: Innovation success depends on how a collective is structured, particularly its level of search dependence and goal alignment. Three main types emerge. Convergence-based collectives involve shared goals and tightly interdependent work, requiring diverse expertise, strong communication, and leadership to integrate ideas into unified solutions. Divergence-based collectives feature participants with different goals operating within a shared network; innovation comes from varied perspectives, but leaders must limit overload and build the capacity to absorb external knowledge. Attention-based collectives combine shared goals with independent work, where individuals explore solutions in parallel; preserving autonomy is crucial because too much visibility into others’ ideas can reduce originality.
